lesson.title: Why the Average of a Sine Wave Is Zero, and What to Do About It
lesson.summary: The plain time average of a full sinusoidal cycle is exactly zero because the positive and negative halves cancel, so power electronics instead defines a rectified average that actually captures the DC content of a signal.
lesson.body:
The average value of a periodic waveform is defined formally as the area under the curve over one full period divided by the period itself, average = (1/T) times the integral of v(t) dt from 0 to T. For a plain sinusoid v(t) = Vm sin(omega t), that integral works out to exactly zero over a full period, because the positive half cycle and the negative half cycle are mirror images of each other and cancel perfectly. This is not a special property of any particular sinusoid, it is true for every sine or cosine wave with no DC offset, regardless of its amplitude or frequency.

A flat zero average is mathematically correct but practically useless whenever the goal is to describe how much genuinely one directional, DC like content a signal carries, which is exactly the question power supply and rectifier design needs answered. The standard fix is to define the average of the rectified waveform instead, either the full-wave rectified average, where every negative excursion is flipped positive before averaging, or the half-wave average, where only the positive half is kept and the negative half is treated as zero. For a sinusoid with peak value Vm, the full-wave rectified average works out to (2/pi) times Vm, about 0.6366 times the peak, and the half-wave rectified average is half of that, (1/pi) times Vm, about 0.3183 times the peak.

Take the household outlet's peak value from two chapters back, Vm = 169.71 V, and pass it through a full-wave rectifier, the kind built from four diodes in a bridge configuration that is standard in AC to DC power supplies. The rectified average is average = (2/pi) times Vm = 0.63662 times 169.71 = 108.04 V. Working through the multiplication directly: 169.71 times 0.6 = 101.83, plus 169.71 times 0.03662 = 6.21, giving a total of 101.83 + 6.21 = 108.04 V, matching the direct calculation.

That 108.04 V average is roughly what a simple rectifier and filter capacitor stage would try to deliver as a DC output from that same 120 V RMS wall outlet, before any additional regulation smooths out the ripple. Notice how this whole calculation was expressed as a fraction of the peak value from the earlier chapter, 0.6366 times Vm, which is exactly why average value was built to depend on peak value in the first place: once you know how high a waveform climbs, the rectified average follows from a single fixed constant that depends only on the waveform's shape, not on how you scale it.

It is worth remembering which average is being discussed in any given context. Say average value about a raw AC sinusoid with no qualification, and the honest answer is zero. Say average value about the same sinusoid after rectification, and the answer becomes a specific nonzero fraction of the peak, 0.6366 Vm for full wave or 0.3183 Vm for half wave, which is almost always the number engineers actually care about.
